Counsellor's note, Thursday.
Tejas, a second-year hostel resident, came to my office at 4 pm holding his phone out as if it were hot. He had paid 1,500 rupees as a 'registration fee' for a work-from-home typing job advertised in a chat group. This morning the recruiter asked for 4,000 more to 'unlock' his earnings.
He said, 'If I pay once more I get it all back, right?' Then he stopped himself. 'No. That's exactly how they keep you paying.'
We took screenshots of every message and the payment receipt together. He called the bank on the number printed on his card and asked them to flag the transfer, then phoned his mother on speaker. He was red in the face but steady.
Next step: he files a complaint on the cybercrime portal tonight. I will check in with him tomorrow morning.
- Vinita, student counsellor

qa.a: He had paid 1,500 rupees as a registration fee for a work-from-home typing job advertised in a chat group.

qa.a: It suggests he was tempted to chase the lost money and hoped one more payment would undo it, though his next words show he saw the trap.

qa.q: What turning point does Tejas take at this stage, and why is it wise?
qa.a: He stops paying, saves the evidence and contacts his bank and his mother; losing 1,500 rupees hurts far less than sending 4,000 more to the same people.

qa.q: What might Tejas's mother be experiencing when he calls her on speaker?
qa.a: She may feel a jolt of worry, but hearing him explain calmly after already calling the bank could reassure her that he trusted her enough to tell her the same day.

Sat, 11 pm
Paid 800 this afternoon for two festival passes from a 'seller' on a resale page. At 7 came the next message: 'Pay 1,200 courier + verification or lose the passes AND your 800.'
My thumb was actually on the pay button. Then I heard myself think: Vandana, if you pay again you're just digging a bigger hole.
So I stopped. Screenshotted the whole chat, the seller's page, the payment ID. The page vanished an hour later, which kind of answered everything.
Called the helpline number printed on my bank card. They flagged it and told me to file a complaint, so I did that too.
Then the hard part: I called Madhuri Masi. She didn't laugh. She just said, 'Good that you stopped at 800.'
Still feel sick about the money. But 800 is where it ends.

qa.a: The seller demanded 1,200 for courier and verification, or else Vandana would lose the passes and the 800.

qa.a: Vandana felt torn: she wanted to protect the 800 already spent, but also saw that paying again would only dig a bigger hole.

qa.a: Stopping before the second payment mattered most; saving the chat and payment ID and calling the number on the card then gave the best chance of limiting harm.

In the small town of Sinnar, Irawati had paid ₹1,500 on Monday to a caller who promised a cheap loan for her tailoring shop under a "government scheme". On Wednesday he called again. "Madam, your file is stuck. Pay ₹6,000 processing fee today, or the first amount is forfeited."
Irawati's stomach turned. Losing the fifteen hundred felt unbearable; it was a week of stitching blouses. But the word forfeited sounded wrong coming from a government office.
She said she would call back and walked straight to Jyoti didi, who ran the women's self-help group from the room behind the temple. Jyoti didi read the messages and shook her head. "Beti, the fifteen hundred is gone. Don't send the six thousand after it."
They took screenshots of every message and the payment slip. Jyoti didi went with her to the bank branch that afternoon, and the manager helped them file a complaint with the cyber-crime helpline.

qa.q: When did Irawati pay the first amount?
qa.a: On Monday.

qa.q: What was Irawati feeling when the caller said the first amount would be forfeited?
qa.a: She felt sick with worry, because losing a week's stitching money felt unbearable, yet the word sounded wrong.

qa.q: What made Irawati's response wise?
qa.a: She paused, went to Jyoti didi, accepted the first loss, kept screenshots and went to the bank the same afternoon to report it.

qa.q: What might Jyoti didi feel reading the messages?
qa.a: Jyoti didi likely feels protective and firm, having seen such tricks before, and wants to stop Irawati losing more.

grounding: A young woman who has already paid a fake loan fee stops, keeps the evidence and goes to the bank with a trusted elder, accepting the first loss.

Gabriel had found the flat in Lisbon online: bright, near the university, cheap. The landlord, who said he was working in Switzerland, sent photos, a scanned passport and a rental contract. Gabriel sent a deposit of four hundred euros.
Two days later the landlord wrote: "Keys are with the agency. Send one more month's rent today, or I give the flat to another student and the deposit is lost."
Gabriel sat in the university café, typing and deleting. Four hundred euros was his whole summer job.
Ingrid, from his Portuguese class, looked at the screen. "Have you seen the flat? In person?"
"No."
She was quiet. Then: "I think the four hundred is gone. Please don't send more."
He felt sick. But he took screenshots, called his bank on the number from his card, and they walked together to the police station on the corner to report it. That night he called his mother and told her everything.

qa.q: How much deposit did Gabriel send?
qa.a: Four hundred euros.

qa.q: What was Gabriel feeling as he typed and deleted in the café?
qa.a: He felt torn and panicked, desperate not to lose his summer job money but sensing something was wrong.

qa.q: Why is stopping at the first loss the right choice?
qa.a: Sending more rent would only grow the loss; screenshots, the bank, the police report and telling his mother give the best chance to limit harm.

qa.q: What might Ingrid have felt saying the four hundred is gone?
qa.a: Ingrid likely felt sorry for Gabriel and uneasy delivering hard news, but sure it would spare him more pain.

grounding: A student who has already paid a fake rental deposit stops, keeps the messages, calls his bank and tells a trusted adult.
